blocks.text: So much for the first irruption of the locusts into Judaea, Amos IV, 9. When this had not moved the Israelites to repentance (The gazam גזם ate your gardens, etc., says the Lord, yet you have not returned to me), God sent other locusts, of which the Prophet speaks thus in chapter 7, verse 1: Thus the Lord showed me. And behold! he was forming locusts when the second-crop hay had sprung up; and the hay was after the king's mowings. Second-crop hay, in Hebrew לקש, usually comes up in Italy in autumn. Columella, on lambs, book 8, chapter 3: They are most conveniently fed on autumn hay, which is called cordum. Aristotle and Pliny teach us that locusts lay their eggs at that very season of the year. The former, History book 5, chapter 28: Τίκτουσι δὲ λήγοντος τοῦ θέρους [Tiktousi de lēgontos tou therous], They lay at the end of summer (not of spring, as Gaza has it). The latter, book 11, chapter 29: These lay, etc., in the autumn season. And that birth is indeed natural, like that of the other animals. The Philosopher teaches this at length in the same place; the sum of it is that the females about to lay fix in the ground τὸν πρὸς τῇ κέρκῳ αὐλὸν [ton pros tē kerkō aulon], the little stalk which they have at the tail, and that towards the end of summer they all deposit their young in the same place, so that they look like a honeycomb. Nor are these committed to the surface of the earth, but to the cracks and fissures with which the ground gapes. When they have lain hidden there all winter, at the beginning of summer they emerge [col. 485] as black worms in the form of eggs, after a thin layer of earth, by which they are enclosed as by a little membrane, has burst. Of this Pliny has only the following: These lay in the ground, letting down the stalk of their spine, eggs packed together in the autumn season. These last through the winter under the ground; and at the end of the following spring they release small, blackish young without legs and wings. And a little later, following others: Others report a double brood and a twofold emergence: that they lay at the rising of the Pleiades, then die at the rising of the Dog Star, and others are born again. Some say they are born again at the setting of Arcturus. That is, as climates vary, so too the time of birth and of death varies for locusts. On this same subject you may read much among the Arabs. Damir: وهو اذا اراد ان يبيض التمس لبيضه المواضع الصلدة والصخور الصلبة التي لا تعمل فيها المعاول فيضربها بذنبه فتفرج له ثم يلقي بيضه في ذلك الصدع فيكون له الافحوص ويكون حاضنا لها ومربيا [wa-huwa idhā arāda an yabīḍa iltamasa li-bayḍihi al-mawāḍiʿ al-ṣalda wa-al-ṣukhūr al-ṣulba allatī lā taʿmalu fīhā al-maʿāwil fa-yaḍribuhā bi-dhanabihi fa-tanfariju lahu thumma yulqī bayḍahu fī dhālika al-ṣadʿ fa-yakūnu lahu al-ufḥūṣ wa-yakūnu ḥāḍinan lahā wa-murabbiyan] When the locust is about to lay, it chooses rough places for its eggs, and very hard rocks which iron has not touched, and [III, 323] beats them with its tail until they open into a crack. Then it lays its eggs in that crack, and this serves it as a nest in which it warms and rears its young. But Alkazuinius has it otherwise: وانا رعت ايام الربيع طلبت ارض طيبة التربة رخوة ونزلت هناك وحفرت باذنابها حفرا وباضت فيها كل واحد ماية بيضة وطارت [wa-anā raʿat ayyām al-rabīʿ ṭalabat arḍ ṭayyibat al-turba rikhwa wa-nazalat hunāka wa-ḥafarat bi-adhnābihā ḥufaran wa-bāḍat fīhā kull wāḥid māyat bayḍa wa-ṭārat] When they graze in springtime, they seek the ground of fertile and soft land, into which they descend; and with their tails they dig pits, in which, when each has laid a hundred eggs, they fly away from there. Close to this number of eggs comes Ibno Omar, when he tells the tale that locusts fell into the hands of Muhammad, on whose wings was written: نحن جند الله الاكبر لنا تسعة وتسعون بيضة ولو تمت لنا الماية لاكلنا الدنيا بما فيها [naḥnu jund Allāh al-akbar lanā tisʿa wa-tisʿūn bayḍa wa-law tammat lanā al-māya la-akalnā al-dunyā bi-mā fīhā] We are the army of the great God. We have ninety-nine eggs; and if the hundred were completed, we would consume the whole world and whatever is in it. There follows in Alkazuinius: ثم اذا اتي ايام الربيع واعتدل الزمان شققت البيض المدفون فظهرت مثل الدبيب الصغار علي وجه الارض فاكلت زرعها حتي قويت ثم نهضت الي بيض اخر وباضت كما فعلت في العام الاول [thumma idhā atā ayyām al-rabīʿ wa-iʿtadala al-zamān shuqqiqat al-bayḍ al-madfūn fa-ẓaharat mithl al-dabīb al-ṣighār ʿalā wajh al-arḍ fa-akalat zarʿahā ḥattā qawiyat thumma nahaḍat ilā bayḍ ākhar wa-bāḍat kamā faʿalat fī al-ʿām al-awwal] Then [col. 486] in springtime, when the season is milder, that buried egg splits, and from it there emerges a kind of small creeping thing on the face of the earth, which eats its crops, until, grown stronger with age, it proceeds to another laying and lays eggs, as had been done the preceding year. In the Alcamus, سرا [srā] sara, and قصم [qṣm] kasam, and مكن [mkn] machin is the egg of the locust; مزكوت [mzkwt] mazcuth is a pregnant locust; متح [mtḥ] mathaha, or متخ [mtkh] mathacha, سخت [skht] sachatha, زر [zr] zarra, and قلز [qlz] kallaza are so many words used of the locust when غرزت ذنبها في الارض لتبيض [gharazat dhanabahā fī al-arḍ li-tabīḍa] it fixes its tail in the ground in order to lay eggs. The locust itself is called صفرا [ṣafrā] saphra when it has laid its eggs, because it is then yellow. The young itself, newly hatched, is دبا [dabā] daba, and دبر [dbr] dabar, and قمص [qmṣ] kamas. Although it is sufficiently clear from this that locusts are formed by Nature, the Prophet nevertheless attributes the formation of the locusts to God. He was forming, he says, locusts, when the second-crop hay first came up. And he uses the verb יצר, which Moses employs where the formation of man and of the other animals is treated in the creation account, Gen. II, 7. 8. 19. Not as if God had created locusts anew after that first production of all things; nor to attribute something peculiar to locusts, as do the petty theologians of the Muslims, who tell the tale that God fashioned locusts من الطين التي فضلت من [III, 324] خلق ادم عليه السلام [min al-ṭīn allatī faḍalat min khalq Ādam ʿalayhi al-salām] from the (better) clay which was left over from the creation of Adam, on whom be peace. Rather, the formation of locusts is attributed to God when they are fertile beyond the usual and multiply immeasurably. For this does not happen without the special providence of God, who uses them as a punishment for sins. Thus this is one of the threats of the divine Law, Deut. XXVIII, 38. You shall cast much seed into the field, and gather little; for the locust shall consume it. And in verse 42: All your trees and the fruits of your land the locust shall possess (as it were) by right of inheritance. Accordingly God speaks thus in 2 Paral. VII, 13. If I command the locust to consume the land. Such is what we read of the Egyptians in Psal. LXXVIII, 46. He (God) gave their produce to the bruchus, and their labour to the locust. And Psal. CV, 34. He (God) spoke, and the locust came, and the bruchus without number. Hence not only the Hebrews but also the Arabs call locusts the army of God, as was observed above ^{c)} on Ioel II, 25. And they tell the tale that, as their Prophet sat with Abdalla, a locust fell onto their table with this inscription on its back and wings: انا الله لا اله الا انا رب الجراد وزارقها ان شيت بعثتها رزقا القوم وان شيت بعثتها بلا علي القوم [anā Allāh lā ilāha illā anā rabb al-jarād wa-zāriquhā in shiʾtu baʿathtuhā rizqan al-qawm wa-in shiʾtu baʿathtuhā balāʾ ʿalā al-qawm] I am God, and there is none besides me, the lord of the locusts, who feed them and, when I please, send them forth to be food for peoples; but also, when I please, send them forth to be a plague upon them.
